extracted.intended_audience: prospective contestants, fans, and researchers of reality television formats
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, format elements, and procedural criteria governing auditions, intermediate rounds, live shows, voting, and prizes on the television competition America’s Got Talent. Covers what acts must do in each stage (time limits, buzzer use, Golden Buzzer, wildcards, voting mechanics, prize options) and how advancement is decided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producers' Auditions (first stage; open to all acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each year's competition begins with the 'Producers' Auditions', conducted across various cities in the United States; this stage is open to all forms of acts and is judged by an independent group to determine who will take part in the Judges' Auditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in multiple cities; functions as a preliminary filtering by producers (not the televised judges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' Auditions — 90 seconds, live audience, buzzer use, majority vote
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Judges' Auditions participants are given 90 seconds to demonstrate their act with a live audience present. Each judge has a buzzer they may use during a performance; if a participant is buzzed by all judges the performance is automatically over. After the performance judges give feedback and a vote; a participant requires a majority vote approving their performance to proceed to the next stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many acts that move on may still be cut due to limited slots for the next stage; participants are held offstage in a waiting room and given a number denoting performance order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online/video auditions (YouTube/MySpace) as alternative entry path
rubrics_metrics.description: From certain seasons acts who did not attend live auditions could submit a taped audition online (e.g., YouTube or MySpace); acts from online auditions were then selected to compete in front of the judges and a live audience during live shows or earlier audition episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The availability and exact mechanics of online submissions varied by season; at one point YouTube registration guaranteed placement in the competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Buzzer — single-usage power that advances acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Golden Buzzer (introduced in season 9) allows a judge to send an act automatically into the live shows regardless of the opinion of the other judges. Initially it saved an act from elimination; its function evolved to grant direct advancement to live shows. A judge may use it only once per season. The host was later allowed to use the Golden Buzzer (from season 11), and guest judges in Judge Cuts have been allowed to use it in some seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules about who may use it and its effect have changed across seasons; usage is limited (one use per judge per season) and has been extended to host/guest judges in later formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-round formats (boot camp / Las Vegas Callbacks / Vegas Verdicts / Judgment Week)
rubrics_metrics.description: After auditions, judges conduct a second session (format has varied): boot camp-style 'Las Vegas Callbacks' (training and re-performance), 'Vegas Verdicts' (judges review audition footage and allocate spaces without re-performing), and 'Judgment Week' (deliberation and elimination). The procedural goal is to determine which participants secure places in the live rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The format has changed multiple times across seasons and may include training, grouping, re-performances, or review-only selection; buzzers could still be used to terminate re-performances under some formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge Cuts — grouped judging with guest judges and Golden Buzzer opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Cuts divided participants into groups judged at a fixed venue, typically with a special guest judge per group. Main judges could still use buzzers to stop performances; the guest judge was allowed to use a Golden Buzzer for a participant they particularly liked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Cuts format and guest-judge usage changed over seasons (e.g., season 15 condensed with no guest judge due to COVID-19; later seasons reverted to a format matching Britain's Got Talent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Live Rounds — new performances, public voting, advancement structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants who reach the live rounds perform new acts before judges and viewers. After each performance episode the public has a set period to vote; results are revealed in a separate 'results' episode. Those with the highest public votes (e.g., Top 4) advance directly; mid-range acts undergo a judges' vote to determine who advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance outfits from the performance episode are worn for results; judges can still give feedback and use buzzers; structures (quarter-finals, semi-finals, finals) and number of finalists have varied by season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' vote for mid-range acts and tiebreak rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For the two acts that receive the mid-range of votes the judges vote to determine which act joins those who advanced. When four judges are present and the judges' vote ties, the act with the higher number of public votes moves on (tie-break to public vote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of judges' vote for advancement was not present in all seasons and its mechanics have evolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wildcard selection — judges' and public's power to reinstate acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts eliminated earlier in the competition may still be appointed as that round's 'Wildcard'. The selection method varied historically; since season 10 the format is more structured, with both judges and the public able to choose Wildcard acts. The public may vote online for an act within each quarter-final and semi-final to move on as a Wildcard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules about whether judges can pick quarter-finalists and exact mechanics have changed season-to-season; Wildcard votes have sometimes been sponsor-branded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-save mechanics (Snapple Vote / Dunkin' Save / sponsor-branded online saves)
rubrics_metrics.description: The show introduced online/sponsor-branded votes (e.g., 'Snapple Vote', later 'Dunkin' Save') allowing the public to save mid-ranking contestants. The scope of these saves has changed (season 10 expanded to cover quarter-finalists finishing 6th–8th and semi-finalists finishing 4th–6th).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics tied to sponsors and evolved across seasons; used to give audiences direct influence over which mid-ranked acts continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of buzzers — judges indicate disapproval and can terminate performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Each judge is given a buzzer and may use it during a performance if they are unimpressed, dislike the act, or feel it is a waste of time. If all buzzers are used the performance is terminated immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buzzers are used both in auditions and live rounds; buzzer use is accompanied by judges' feedback when performances end naturally or are stopped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time/venue logistics and staging (performance order, waiting room, presenter role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants reaching Judges' Auditions are held offstage in a waiting room, given a number denoting when they will perform, and the presenter stands in the wings to interview and give personal commentary. Live episodes are held within set venues (location varied), with a live audience present for auditions and performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auditions and filming schedules take place months before broadcast; venues for live rounds have changed by season (e.g., moved to Los Angeles or Radio City Music Hall depending on season and judge schedules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and scope of acts — any age/location/format
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept permits participants of any age and location to enter with any form of talent they choose to perform (singing, dancing, comedy, magic, stunts, variety, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to be broadly inclusive of act types; however, practical constraints (safety, venue, legal/production) affect acceptance and staging of some acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize structure and winner entitlements (cash, annuity, Las Vegas headlining, next-season appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The winner is advertised as receiving $1 million, but in reality winners can choose either a lump sum or a financial annuity paid out over forty years (~$25,000/year); both options are subject to taxation. Since the third season winners also received a chance to headline a show on the Las Vegas Strip (with some exceptions), and since Season 10 the winner performs on the first results show of the next season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize presentation in advertising differs from practical payout options; additional prizes (headline shows, tours) have varied across seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of dangerous/‘extreme’ acts — special audition sessions and safety accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: Season 10 included a special 'extreme' audition session held on an outdoor stage for participants with acts considered too dangerous for an indoor studio set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production may create separate audition processes or venues to accommodate safety concerns and insurance/logistical constraints for risky performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format evolution and season-specific rule changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Format elements (e.g., Golden Buzzer usage, Judge Cuts structure, Wildcard mechanics, which roles may use the Golden Buzzer, public vote windows, guest-judge participation) have changed across seasons in response to production choices and external circumstances (e.g., COVID-19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitors and producers must consult the current season's rules because many procedural details are season-specific and have evolved over time.
